segments.say: Lesson 17. Memory & Context Engineering. Short-term versus long-term memory, summarization, and deciding what goes into the context window.

L L Ms remember nothing between calls. Memory is your app deciding what past information (recent messages, summaries, saved facts) to put back into each prompt. This is called context engineering. Here is an analogy. A doctor with no memory but excellent notes: before each visit they read the latest notes, a summary of your history and your allergies. What goes in the notes decides the quality of care.

Why does this matter? Every chatbot and agent needs it. Bad memory means a forgetful bot or a huge, expensive, confused prompt. A few key words. Short-term memory: The current conversation thread. Long-term memory: Facts saved across sessions. Summarisation: Compressing old messages. Context engineering: Choosing exactly what goes into the context window.

segments.say: Context engineering equals filling the window with the right information in the right format, at minimum tokens. It's the core skill behind reliable agents.

Types of memory. Short-term (working): the current thread's messages and state. Long-term semantic: facts about the user or world ("works on Verizon project"). Episodic: past interactions and outcomes ("last time this alert was a false positive"), useful as few-shot examples. Procedural: learned instructions and rules, sometimes the agent updating its own system prompt.

Strategies. Sliding window (last N messages), token-based trimming. Summary memory (running summary plus recent turns). Vector memory: embed past memories and retrieve by similarity. Entity memory: a structured profile per entity. Write memory either in the hot path (the agent calls save memory as a tool) or in the background (a reflection job after the conversation).

Gotchas. Context rot: overly long contexts degrade quality. More isn't better. Stale or contradictory memories, so you need update and delete logic. Privacy: P I I retention, user consent and deletion requests.

Say it in the interview. "L L Ms are stateless, so memory is a context-engineering problem. Short-term memory is thread state persisted by a checkpointer, trimmed or summarized to a token budget. Long-term memory lives in a store, written by the agent or a background reflection job, and retrieved by relevance. I watch for staleness, contradictions and P I I.".

Let's compare. Full history: everything, perfect recall, token blowup, context rot. Sliding window: last N turns, simple, bounded, forgets early facts. Summary: summary plus recent, bounded, keeps gist, lossy, extra L L M calls. Vector memory: embedded past snippets, scales, relevance-based, retrieval misses. Structured profile: key facts per user, precise, editable, needs extraction logic.

A likely interview question: What is context engineering? A strong answer: Deciding what goes into the model's context window each step (instructions, memory, retrieved docs, tool results), in what format, within a token budget. It's the main lever for agent reliability.
That's it for Memory & Context Engineering. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
